planting.note: Set out after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; deadhead spent blooms to prolong the long flowering season.

directions: A heavy-blooming sun daisy selection smothered in pure white, dark-eyed, daisy-like flowers from spring through late summer on a compact, mounding plant. It tolerates more cold and drought than typical florist-type osteospermums, making it viable as a reliable perennial in colder xeriscape gardens rather than strictly an annual bedding plant. Well-drained soil and full sun keep bloom production at its peak.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this Mexicali-series hybrid blooms over an especially long season.

directions: One of the Mexicali series of hybrid penstemons combining the large, showy flowers of tender Mexican species with the hardiness of native American ones, this selection bears soft pink blooms over silvery foliage from late spring well into fall. It blooms longer than most native penstemons and tolerates heat and drought with ease. Sharp winter drainage is important, since the hybrid's Mexican parentage makes it less tolerant of wet, cold soil than pure native species.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this Mexicali-series hybrid forms a tidy, floriferous mound.

directions: A Mexicali-series hybrid beardtongue bearing rosy-purple tubular flowers over a long bloom season from late spring through fall, held above neat gray-green foliage. Its compact, rounded habit suits smaller borders and rock gardens where taller penstemons would overwhelm nearby plants. Good drainage and lean soil help it persist through winter better than it would in rich, moisture-retentive beds.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; deadheading spent spikes encourages continued bloom.

directions: A Mexicali-series penstemon with deep garnet-red tubular flowers held on upright spikes above fine gray-green foliage, blooming from late spring into fall and drawing hummingbirds throughout. It is taller and more vigorous than many compact penstemon selections, giving it good presence in a mixed xeriscape border. Lean, sharply drained soil in full sun keeps it healthy through winter.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; it spreads gradually into a glowing low mat.

directions: A low, spreading native prairie plant covered through much of the summer in bright golden-yellow, four-petaled flowers that open in late afternoon and glow at dusk, a characteristic shared with its evening primrose relatives. Its fine, needle-like green foliage forms a dense weed-smothering mat in hot, dry sites where few other groundcovers thrive. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and needs no deadheading to keep flowering.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in lean, sharply drained soil; avoid rich soils, which cause lanky, weak growth.

directions: A tidy, evergreen-stemmed shrub native to the high mountains of Spain (long sold under the older name Cytisus purgans), densely covered in bright golden-yellow pea-like flowers in late spring that perfume the air. Its fine, nearly leafless green stems keep the plant looking evergreen through winter even without foliage. It thrives in lean, rocky soil and resents the rich, well-watered conditions that make many brooms rangy and short-lived.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this New Mexico native is sparse-foliaged, so site it among fuller companions.

directions: A New Mexico native figwort bearing tall, airy spikes of small, brick-red, bird-like flowers that dangle from wiry stems like a row of perched red birds, a magnet for hummingbirds through summer. Its sparse, open habit and modest foliage mean it is best planted among bushier xeriscape companions rather than alone. It is extremely drought tolerant once established, thriving in the same lean, gravelly soils as its wild high-desert habitat.

planting.note: Plant small divisions in spring in gritty, well-drained soil between pavers or in a lawn alternative planting.

directions: A selection of low-growing native pussytoes forming a tight, silvery-gray evergreen mat ideal as a short, drought-proof lawn alternative or filler between stepping stones. Fuzzy, cat's-paw-like flower clusters appear briefly in spring, but the fine silver foliage carries interest the rest of the year. It tolerates foot traffic, extreme drought, and poor soil better than almost any other groundcover.

planting.note: Set out after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; established plants rebloom reliably each spring and summer.

directions: A sun daisy selection introduced in memory of a longtime program supporter, producing abundant purple-pink, dark-centered daisy flowers over a compact mound from spring through summer. It is hardier than typical bedding osteospermums, allowing it to return as a genuine perennial in milder xeriscape gardens rather than needing annual replacement. Full sun and sharp drainage keep it blooming at its best.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; this dwarf form stays tighter than the standard species.

directions: An unusually small, tight selection of needle-leaf penstemon that packs the same bright orange-red tubular flowers and evergreen needle-like foliage of the standard species into a miniature scale suited to troughs, small rock gardens, and tight crevices. It blooms over a long summer season and tolerates extreme drought once rooted. Sharp drainage is essential, since its reduced size offers little buffer against soggy soil.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; it spreads into a flat, radiating mat reminiscent of wagon-wheel spokes.

directions: A mat-forming native penstemon selection that hugs the ground tightly, radiating outward in a flat carpet of small gray-green leaves smothered in lavender-blue flowers in late spring. Its extremely low, spreading habit makes it ideal for covering ground between stepping stones or cascading over rock walls. It is highly drought tolerant and resents any standing winter moisture.

planting.note: Set out after last frost in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; harvest leaves and flower spikes in summer for tea.

directions: A selection of the Greek herb traditionally brewed as mountain tea, forming a mounding subshrub of soft, felted silvery-green leaves and upright spikes of small yellow flowers favored by bees. Beyond its ornamental silver foliage, the aromatic leaves and flowering tops can be dried for a mild, herbal infusion. It needs excellent winter drainage and is less reliably hardy than fully xeric Rocky Mountain natives.

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this high-elevation native thrives at cooler sites.

directions: A selection of a Rocky Mountain alpine fleabane producing cheerful lavender-pink daisy flowers with yellow centers over a low mound of narrow green leaves through much of summer. Its naturally compact, spreading habit suits rock gardens and front-of-border plantings at higher elevations where many lowland perennials struggle. It tolerates cold, wind, and lean soil typical of its subalpine meadow origins.

planting.note: Plant in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this Pyrenees native needs much better drainage than bedding snapdragons.

directions: A true perennial snapdragon from the Pyrenees, unlike the familiar annual bedding type, forming a tight, woody-based cushion of small gray-green leaves dotted with miniature white-and-yellow snapdragon flowers through summer. Its diminutive scale and cushion habit suit rock garden crevices, troughs, and scree beds. Sharp mineral drainage is essential, since it is far less tolerant of garden-soil moisture than common snapdragons.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; it creeps to form a dense, silvery evergreen mat.

directions: A low, spreading germander selection with small, silvery, evergreen leaves that creep outward to form a dense, year-round mat ideal for edging or cascading over rock walls. Small lavender flowers appear in summer but the persistent silver foliage carries the display through every season. It roots easily where stems touch soil and tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease.

planting.note: Set out after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; named for its distinctive curled, caterpillar-like seed heads.

directions: A South African grass selection grown for its unusual curled, fuzzy seed spikes that genuinely resemble small caterpillars perched along arching stems above a neat clump of fine green foliage. Its compact size and novel texture make it a conversation piece in a mixed border or container planting. It is less cold-hardy than most Plant Select introductions and benefits from a sheltered site in colder zones.

planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; it forms an upright clump that needs no staking.

directions: An upright steppe perennial bearing dense spikes of intensely deep indigo-blue, hooded flowers above narrow, aromatic foliage through summer, a vivid color rare among drought-tolerant plants. Its tidy, clumping habit and strong vertical form make it useful for adding structure to a xeriscape border without flopping. It is extremely cold-hardy, reflecting its wide native range across the cold steppes of Europe and Asia.

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this legume relative fixes its own nitrogen and needs little feeding.

directions: A lupine relative producing upright, candle-like spikes of bright golden-yellow pea flowers above handsome, trifoliate blue-green leaves in late spring and early summer. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it thrives in lean soil without supplemental fertilizer, improving the ground around it as it grows. Its sturdy, clumping habit provides strong vertical form in a xeriscape or prairie-style border.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; deadhead to prolong the summer bloom display.

directions: A knapweed relative bearing soft pink, fringed, cornflower-like blooms above tidy gray-green foliage through summer, offering a color rarely seen among drought-tolerant perennials. Its compact, clumping habit works well toward the front of a dry border or rock garden. It tolerates heat and poor soil with ease and attracts bees and butterflies throughout its bloom season.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; expect a strong spring flush followed by lighter repeat bloom.

directions: A compact littleleaf lilac selection bred for extended bloom, opening fragrant pink flower clusters in a strong spring display and continuing with sporadic rebloom through summer rather than flowering only once. Its small, neat leaves and rounded habit suit smaller gardens better than standard lilac shrubs. It is extremely cold-hardy and needs only modest water once established.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this compact selection needs little to no pruning to stay neat.

directions: A tidy, compact selection of the extremely cold-hardy littleleaf peashrub, keeping the fine, ferny foliage and bright yellow pea flowers of the species on a naturally neater, more restrained shrub. As a legume it improves lean soil as it grows and tolerates wind, cold, and drought that would damage less rugged shrubs. It makes a good low hedge or windbreak component on the high plains without the need for frequent shaping.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; give it ample room as it matures into a full-size tree.

directions: An Arizona cypress selection with striking frosty, silvery-blue foliage that intensifies in cold weather, giving strong winter color to an evergreen screen or specimen planting. It grows into a substantial pyramidal tree tolerant of heat, wind, and extended drought once established. Good drainage is essential, since Arizona cypress is intolerant of consistently wet soil.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; its naturally weeping, trailing branches make it suited for cascading over walls.

directions: An unusual weeping selection of native sand cherry discovered growing low and trailing, in contrast to the typical shrubby upright form of the species. Small white spring flowers and edible dark cherries follow the same seasonal pattern as standard sand cherry, but on cascading branches well suited to draping over a wall or raised bed edge. It is extremely cold-hardy and tolerates poor, sandy soil with minimal water.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this nativar selection has notably silvery foliage compared to the wild species.

directions: A selection of a native evening primrose prized for its distinctively silvery-blue foliage, a striking backdrop for the large, cheerful yellow, four-petaled flowers that open over a long summer season. Its low, spreading habit fills in quickly between other xeriscape perennials without becoming aggressive. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and needs no deadheading to keep blooming.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this late-season bloomer provides fall color and nectar when little else is flowering.

directions: A California fuchsia selection bearing a profusion of brilliant orange-red tubular flowers in late summer and fall, a crucial nectar source for migrating hummingbirds heading south. Its gray-green, slightly fuzzy foliage spreads by rhizomes to form a loose groundcover between other dry-garden perennials. It is extremely drought tolerant and benefits from a hard cutback in late winter to keep growth dense.

planting.note: Plant divisions or stem pieces in spring in fast-draining soil; winter cold intensifies the foliage color that gives this selection its name.

directions: A hardy stonecrop selection with blue-green summer foliage that transforms into fiery orange-red tones through fall and winter, giving extended-season color rare among succulent groundcovers. Clusters of small starry yellow flowers appear on upright stems in summer above the colorful foliage mat. It spreads readily in lean, sharply drained soil and tolerates extreme cold and drought with ease.
